it’s all right, don’t be afraid

terms.grammar: nē with the present imperative; to several, Nē timēte!
evidence: Plaut. Amph. 674: Sequere hāc mē modo … nē timē.
Plaut. Rud. 1049: Ego vōs salvās sistam, nē timēte.
Plaut. Mil. 1345: Nē timē, voluptās mea.
terms.comment: What Plautus’s people say again and again to calm someone (also Mercator, Pseudolus, Trinummus), often beside a promise: I’ll see you safe. The imperative with nē belongs to comedy and conversation, and so to a father’s speech; prose writes nōlī timēre.

terms.gloss: don’t be afraid (the plain prose prohibition)
evidence: Vulg. Jo. 6.20: Ego sum, nōlīte timēre.
terms.comment: The ordinary classical way of forbidding. The phrase itself we have found in the Vulgate, not in the comedies or Cicero’s letters, where the prohibition is nē timē.

phrases.english: Don’t be afraid, my boy: I’m here.
Don’t be afraid: the dog doesn’t bite.

phrases.latin: Sequere hāc mē modo; alium ego istī reī allēgābō, nē timē.
phrases.english: Just follow me this way; I’ll put someone else onto that business, don’t be afraid.

phrases.latin: Ego vōs salvās sistam, nē timēte.
phrases.english: I’ll keep you both safe, don’t be afraid.
It is I; do not be afraid.
